clue.text: Joint in dreadfully poor taste? Not quite

indicators.note: something done dreadfully is done badly, so the letters come out in a messed-up order
not quite complete means the final letter of the phrase is dropped before rearranging

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then cut short

explanation.surface: Someone sneers that a cut of meat is in dreadfully poor taste, then half takes it back.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the last E of taste, then rearrange the remaining eight letters of poor tast.
explanation.definitionFit: A pot roast is a cut of beef braised slowly in a covered pan, and a joint is a large cut of meat.

clue.text: Father goes on fast in church office

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father
pacy means fast, full of pace

explanation.surface: A priest keeps a fast while holding an office in the church.
explanation.walkthrough: Fast looks like going without food in a church context, but here it means quick. 'goes on' simply puts one piece after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The papacy is the office and authority of the Pope, the highest position in the Roman Catholic Church.

clue.text: Change direction in act on cycle

blocks.note: a turn is an act in a variety show
a round is a cycle, as in a round of talks

explanation.surface: A performer on a bicycle swings round mid-act.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn round is to face or head the opposite way, reversing one's course.

clue.text: Clothing for protection that's paramount?

blocks.note: first meaning: a loose coat or one-piece garment worn over clothes to keep them clean
second meaning: supreme, ranking above all others

explanation.surface: Asking whether protective clothing is the top priority on a work site.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a protective work garment, and the adjective means total or supreme, as in the overall winner.

clue.text: Did stomach take second lot of food?

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for second
tuck is British schoolboy slang for food, especially sweets and snacks

explanation.surface: Asking whether a hungry eater's belly could manage a second helping.
explanation.walkthrough: Stomach is a verb meaning tolerate, and its past tense is wanted; the surface makes it the belly.
explanation.definitionFit: To stick something is to put up with it, so stuck means tolerated or endured, as in stuck it out.

clue.text: Man, for one, I malign with no hesitation

indicators.note: the hesitation sound er is removed, so those two letters are taken out of the verb

blocks.note: taken as written
to malign someone is to slander them

explanation.surface: A speaker confesses to bad-mouthing someone, and doing it fluently, without a single um or er.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is the written form of the hesitation sound, so it is cut from SLANDER. 'Man' is not a person: it is the Isle of Man.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man in the Irish Sea is an example of a piece of land surrounded by water.

clue.text: Rose was not invalid

blocks.note: first meaning: got to one's feet
second meaning: held good when tested, as an argument does

explanation.walkthrough: Invalid suggests a sick person who could not get up, but it is the adjective meaning unsound.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both got up onto one's feet and survived scrutiny, as evidence that holds in court.

clue.text: Don's familiar with a maiden I serve

blocks.note: taken as written
m is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a maiden over
taken as written
a serve in tennis is one's go, one's turn

explanation.surface: A university don's close companion is a young woman who waits on him.
explanation.walkthrough: Don is the Spanish title, not an Oxford tutor, so his familiar friend is a Spanish word.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is Spanish for friend, so a Spanish gentleman's familiar companion would be his amigo.

clue.text: Heated argument heard before church, perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: a noisy, fierce quarrel
second meaning: the sound of bells pealing to call people to a service

explanation.walkthrough: Heard makes it look like a sound-alike clue, but it is literal: bells are heard ringing before a service.
explanation.definitionFit: The imitative word for a pealing bell is also British slang for a vigorous row or fight.

clue.text: Hero's lamentation in tree

blocks.note: Hero, the priestess of Greek myth, cried out the name of her lover after he drowned swimming the Hellespont to reach her

explanation.surface: A hero mourns while sitting in a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: Hero is not a brave man but the priestess of the myth; her lament is the vocative O followed by her drowned lover's name, Leander.
explanation.definitionFit: The oleander is a poisonous evergreen Mediterranean shrub or small tree with pink or white flowers.

clue.text: Endless debating? It's proved to be impossible

blocks.note: first meaning: a never-ending succession of motions put forward for debate
second meaning: the physicist's machine that runs forever with no energy input

explanation.walkthrough: A motion is a proposal put to a debate, so endless debating is a perpetual stream of them; physics shows a perpetual-motion machine cannot exist.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a hypothetical machine running forever without fuel, which thermodynamics rules out, and punningly a debate whose proposals never stop.

clue.text: Road transport's still here — fish taken by old vessel

blocks.note: a carp is a freshwater fish
Noah's ark, the ancient boat

explanation.surface: A fish is carried off in an old boat while the lorries sit idle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken by' just places the fish before the vessel. 'Still' means motionless: this is where vehicles stand when not moving.
explanation.definitionFit: A car park is an area where motor vehicles are left stationary, the British term for a parking lot.

clue.text: Robot also needs switch I inserted

indicators.note: inserted says one piece is put inside another, here the letter going into the switch

blocks.note: and means also, in addition
a switch is a thin flexible rod or cane
taken as written

explanation.surface: A robot also needs an on-off switch fitted, as if it were an electrical repair job.
explanation.walkthrough: The switch here is not electrical but a cane for beating; I goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An android is a robot built to look and behave like a human being, a staple of science fiction.

clue.text: Disorderly lout given a fright and banned

indicators.note: disorderly means out of order, so those letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
awed means filled with fear or dread

explanation.surface: A disorderly hooligan gets scared off and barred, perhaps from a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Something outlawed has been made illegal or prohibited, the same as being banned.

clue.text: Heads of television in conflict over plan for channel

indicators.note: in places the opening letters inside the word for fighting

blocks.note: war is armed conflict
the first two letters of television, its head
a way is a plan or method of doing something

explanation.surface: Television bosses at odds over plans for a TV channel.
explanation.walkthrough: Over means placed above in a down clue, so the plan comes after. Channel is not a TV station but a canal.
explanation.definitionFit: A waterway is a navigable river or canal, and a channel is a passage of water.

clue.text: Flat and smooth, so to speak

indicators.note: so to speak flags that the word is to be judged by its spoken sound

blocks.note: to plane wood is to smooth it, and the word is pronounced the same as the answer

explanation.surface: Describing a surface, perhaps a table top, as flat and smooth.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain is an expanse of level land, and as an adjective the word means flat or unadorned.

clue.text: Satisfaction that one mentor is concealing

indicators.note: is concealing says the letters sit hidden within the words in front of it

blocks.note: the last letter of 'that' runs on through 'one mentor'

explanation.surface: A teacher's quiet contentment that a pupil is keeping something hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters start with the final A of 'that', which is why 'that' is part of the run as well as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Satisfaction in the old sense is amends or reparation made for a wrong, which is what atonement means.

clue.text: He's prepared to forgive buddy about nothing

indicators.note: about means around, so the friend's name wraps around the zero

blocks.note: pardner is the folksy American form of partner, a mate
the figure zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A forgiving man is willing to excuse a friend who has done nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A pardoner was a medieval cleric licensed to sell indulgences, or anyone who grants forgiveness for wrongs.

clue.text: Hold water that's a degree higher

blocks.note: taken as written
DD, Doctor of Divinity, is a university degree
higher means up

explanation.surface: Water held in a tank is a degree warmer, as if reading a thermometer.
explanation.walkthrough: The degree is not temperature but an academic one, DD. To hold water is the idiom for an argument standing up to scrutiny, as figures do when they add up.
explanation.definitionFit: Both idioms describe an explanation or account that makes sense and is consistent when examined.

clue.text: Wretched disheartened type given religious sanctuary

indicators.note: disheartened means the heart is removed, leaving only the outside letters
given sanctuary means taken in and sheltered, so it goes inside the devout word

blocks.note: pious means devoutly religious
only the first and last letters kept

explanation.surface: A miserable, dispirited person is taken in by a church as a refugee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'religious sanctuary' reads as one phrase, but religious is a piece and sanctuary the instruction to shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: Piteous means deserving or arousing pity, so a piteous state is a wretched one.

clue.text: Killer charged in Spain

blocks.note: surface reading: a murderer formally accused by Spanish police
setter's reading: the bullfighter is the one the bull charges at in the ring

explanation.surface: A murderer has been formally indicted by the courts in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: Charged is the legal sense on the surface but the physical rush of a bull in the cryptic reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A toreador is a bullfighter, a man whose job in the Spanish arena ends with the animal's death after it repeatedly rushes at him.

clue.text: He rebelled against father so, a lamb going astray

indicators.note: going astray means wandering off the right path, so the letters wander out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rebellious son is likened to a lamb that strays from the flock.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Bible, Absalom was the son of King David who led a revolt against him.
explanation.definitionFit: Absalom is the biblical son of King David who raised an army in rebellion against his father.

clue.text: One who's never going to be a persistent competitor?

blocks.note: first meaning: someone who stays put
second meaning: a racehorse or athlete with stamina for long distances

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone who will never make a good competitor; read literally, the first half is a person who never leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: In racing the word names a horse or runner with staying power, and literally anyone who remains rather than departs.

clue.text: Goddess encountered in the herd

indicators.note: in places one word inside the other, the meeting sitting within the animals

blocks.note: deer move in herds, so the herd stands for the animals
met means encountered

explanation.surface: A goddess is met among a herd of animals, like a pastoral myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Demeter is the Greek goddess of the harvest and agriculture, mother of Persephone.

clue.text: Concept upwardly mobile male provided

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat

clue.text: Opposition ends its reforms

indicators.note: reforms means forms again, so these letters are reshaped into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A protest movement stops once its reforms are passed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reforms' reads as a noun on the surface but works as a verb meaning reshapes.

clue.text: Hidden and keeping silent to track game

blocks.note: to dog someone is to track or follow them
go is the Japanese board game

explanation.surface: A hunter stays concealed and quiet in order to follow game animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Game is not hunted animals but the board game; to lie doggo is British slang for staying hidden and still.
explanation.definitionFit: Doggo is informal British slang, chiefly in lie doggo, meaning motionless and quiet so as to escape notice.

clue.text: Countryman runs on board ship — behind Nelson's back, it appears

indicators.note: on board means aboard a vessel, so the runs go inside the ship

blocks.note: a national is a citizen of a country
a galley is an oared ship

explanation.surface: A sailor runs aboard ship and sneaks behind Admiral Nelson's back.
explanation.walkthrough: Nelson's Column stands in Trafalgar Square, London, and this art museum fills the north side of the square behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: The London art museum lies directly behind the statue of Nelson atop his column, so it seems to be at his back.

clue.text: Judge application to be rubbish

blocks.note: a ref, short for referee, judges a game
use means application, as in the use of a tool

explanation.surface: A judge deems a legal application worthless and throws it out.
explanation.definitionFit: Refuse is waste matter thrown away, a formal word for trash or garbage.

clue.text: Traveller who won't go as far as 17?

definitions.text: who won't go as far as 17

blocks.note: first meaning: someone making a regular journey to work

blocks.clueFragment: who won't go as far as 17
blocks.note: second meaning: one who reduces a sentence rather than cancelling it as the forgiver at 17 does

explanation.walkthrough: 17 is PARDONER. To commute a sentence is to lessen it, a step short of a full pardon; the travelling sense hides this.
explanation.definitionFit: A commuter is a daily rail or road traveller, and also someone who lightens a punishment without wiping it out entirely.
